source_document.body:
If you’ve spent the last year watching driverless trucks rack up miles on the lanes you used to run and felt something between anger and dread, that reaction is fair, it’s shared by most of the industry, and it isn’t paranoia, because the deployment timeline that always seemed to sit five years out has quietly collapsed into this quarter and the next one.
Here’s what the industry keeps dancing around. The technology is further along than the skeptics claimed, and the business model behind it has a hole in the middle big enough for a small carrier to drive through.
Where this actually stands
Start with the facts, not the hype.
Aurora launched commercial driverless operations on the Dallas-Houston corridor in April 2025 . By the end of this past January it had logged more than 250,000 driverless miles, and by the end of June that number was close to 440,000. It now runs across 10 driverless routes in the Sun Belt, including a roughly 1,000-mile Fort Worth to Phoenix lane that goes well past what hours of service allows a single driver, and it has said it expects more than 200 driverless trucks in operation by the end of this year.
Kodiak took a different road . It put its system into trucks the customer owns. Atlas Energy Solutions had 20 driverless Kodiak-powered trucks running in the Permian at the end of last year and 35 by the end of June, with more than 40,000 cumulative hours of paid driverless operations. Kodiak is targeting a driverless long-haul launch on Dallas-Houston by the end of 2026.
And this week, Volvo Autonomous Solutions and Waabi started hauling freight for Warp’s LTL networ k on the Dallas-Houston corridor, with an observer still in the seat. Waabi says driverless runs on Volvo’s purpose-built truck start next year, and that it has cut the time to open a new lane from three months to three weeks to, on at least one lane, nothing at all.
That last detail is the one carriers should sit with. The constraint used to be geography. It isn’t anymore.
American truck drivers are about to be replaced at a rapid pace Volvo is ramping up autonomous truck production and has plans to manufacture hundreds of these self driving trucks and start rolling them out onto the highways without safety drivers by the start of next year Volvo… pic.twitter.com/dbsK4d1UXb — Wall Street Apes (@WallStreetApes) October 4, 2026
The anger is earned
Drivers aren’t being unreasonable, and the public isn’t either.
A March poll from Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety found 85% of respondents were concerned about sharing the road with autonomous trucks. A January survey of Illinois voters found 78% opposed allowing driverless heavy trucks in the state. Teamsters California sued the state DMV over its autonomous vehicle rules, arguing the regulations could eventually wipe out the jobs of more than 200,000 employee semi-truck drivers in California, with a similar number of self-employed drivers affected on top of that.
OOIDA has been just as direct, opposing the SELF DRIVE Act of 2026 on the grounds that it would let 80,000-pound driverless trucks deploy largely on company self-certification, without independent federal verification and without clear qualifications for the remote operators overseeing them.
Those are legitimate objections, and small-business truckers have every right to keep pressing them. Fighting for oversight and preparing for the market that exists are not mutually exclusive. Drivers who do only the first and none of the second will get run over by a market that didn’t wait for the argument to finish.
What these networks still can’t do
Every one of these deployments has the same shape. Highway middle mile, terminal to terminal, in good weather, on validated lanes.
What falls outside that? Backing into a tight dock. Working a yard. Dealing with a dock worker who moves you to a different door. Strapping and tarping. Chains. Breakdowns on the shoulder. A reefer that throws a code at 2 a.m. Detention negotiations. The customer who needs the driver to walk the freight inside. Anything that requires judgment, hands, or a conversation.
Even Waabi’s pitch tells you this. Its executives talk about running LTL consolidation on a corridor like Dallas-Houston without hours-of-service limits, which means the middle leg is the target. The pickup and the delivery still belong to somebody. Somebody has to pull the trailer to the launch point and somebody has to take it off the landing point and get it to the customer.
Autonomy doesn’t eliminate that work. It concentrates it.
The part of the model that works in your favor
Here’s the structural thing I’d want every owner-operator to understand.
Kodiak’s business model isn’t selling trucking. It’s Driver as a Service . The company sells access to its system on vehicles the customer owns and operates. That’s how Atlas ended up with its own driverless fleet instead of buying capacity from a tech company.
Read that again, because it goes both ways. If a software company will put its system in a customer-owned truck, then the asset owner still matters. The question for small carriers isn’t whether a robot can drive. It’s whether, five years from now, the trucks running these lanes are owned by three tech-backed giants or by a thousand American carriers who figured out how to buy the technology instead of competing against it.
Nobody’s handing a one-truck owner-operator a driverless unit next spring. The capital, the insurance, the lane validation and the maintenance requirements are all real. But the model that puts the asset in the carrier’s name is already operating commercially, and carriers who understand it now will be at the front of the line when the entry cost falls, the way it fell on every other piece of trucking technology.
The businesses that get built around this
Beyond ownership, there’s a service economy forming around these networks, and most of it needs people with CDLs and shop experience. A few avenues worth looking at.
Drayage into and out of transfer points. Every autonomous lane needs a first and last leg. That’s day-cab work, home every night, repeatable, and it’s exactly the kind of local lane that pairs well with a direct shipper relationship rather than a load board.
Yard and hostling contracts. Someone has to spot trailers, move equipment, and keep the lot flowing. Autonomous networks make yards busier, not emptier.
Recovery and roadside response. When an autonomous unit goes down, somebody local has to get to it fast. Tire service, jump starts, towing coordination, sensor cleaning, securing a load that shifted. That’s a contract business for an operator with the right equipment and a service mindset.
Remote oversight and fleet monitoring. OOIDA’s own objection points at the opening here, since the qualifications for remote operators of commercial vehicles are still unsettled. The people best qualified to oversee a truck remotely are people who have driven one. If that role gets a federal standard, experienced drivers should be first in line, and they should be pushing for that standard now.
Trailer pools and equipment leasing. These networks need boxes, and plenty of them. Owning trailers that run inside an autonomous network is a way to earn off the technology without driving the lane yourself.
Maintenance, upfitting and calibration. Kodiak partners with commercial upfitters to install its hardware because OEMs aren’t producing driverless-ready trucks at scale yet. Sensor calibration and AV preventive maintenance are new line items in every shop that wants them.
Freight autonomy isn’t built for. Flatbed and heavy haul. Hazmat. Final mile and white glove. Local and regional work with handling. Construction and aggregate. Anything where the driver is doing more than steering is freight these systems aren’t touching anytime soon.
Why it matters
The honest version of this story isn’t that autonomy is harmless, and it isn’t that drivers are about to be erased. It’s that the work is being restructured, and restructuring always moves the money. Long-haul middle mile is getting automated first because it’s the easiest piece and the one drivers like least. Everything hard, local and human-dependent is getting more valuable as a result.
The drivers who lose here will be the ones who kept running the exact lane a machine was built to run, with no shipper relationships, no local footprint and no plan. The ones who win will be the ones who saw the whole network, found the part of it that still needs hands and judgment, and charged accordingly.
American truckers have been told to adapt for 40 years, usually by people who have never backed into a dock. This is different, because for the first time the technology is being sold in a form that lets the carrier own the asset.

Fit Energy, a developer of energy solutions for data center projects, has announced plans for a fuel cell power generation and data center project in Newport Township, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania. The project received township zoning approval for both uses in August of this year. Fit Energy on October 6 said engineering and the remaining permitting work are now underway ahead of construction.
The project is planned on land that has already been mined and quarried, putting previously used industrial property back into productive use rather than developing untouched forests or farmland. The on-site power will be generated by natural gas fuel cells supplied by FuelCell Energy, Inc., a Connecticut-based manufacturer of utility-scale fuel cell technology, under its strategic agreement with Fit Energy .
The fuel cells produce electricity through an electrochemical process rather than combustion, which helps deliver cleaner energy with minimal impact on the surrounding community. On-site power generation will reduce the project’s reliance on the regional power grid.
The site plan includes setbacks, landscaping, and screening designed to limit views of the site from nearby homes and local roads, demonstrating a focus on balancing energy infrastructure needs with community character.
The project includes investment in power, natural gas, water, and sewer infrastructure that will serve the site and add to local utility capacity and stability for the future. Construction is expected to create significant employment and business opportunities for contractors, skilled trades, and suppliers over a multi-year buildout. Once operational, the project is expected to support permanent skilled positions in operations, maintenance, security, facility management, and technology. The project is also expected to generate new tax revenue for Newport Township, the local school district, and Luzerne County.
Fit Energy is working with Newport Township on a Community Benefits Agreement that would create a formal framework for directing additional investment toward priorities identified by the community.
“The Newport Township Commissioners have been proactive in their response to promote development in appropriately zoned sections of the Township that respects community input and promotes investments that create new jobs and new local tax revenue that enhance the quality of life for all Township residents,” said Joe Hillan, Newport Township Manager. “We recognize Fit Energy has made significant commitment to this development, and we welcome the company’s investment in our community and appreciate Fit Energy’s willingness to work with the Township to address any and all community concerns.”
Fit Energy said it will work closely with township officials and residents through permitting, construction, and operations. As part of that commitment, Fit Energy will host a public information session where residents can review the plans, ask questions, and hear directly from the project team. The date, time, and location will be announced at www.newportdatacenter.com, where residents can also submit questions, read answers to frequently asked questions, and follow project updates.
“A project like this is most successful when the community has the opportunity to hear directly from the people building it,” said Joel Leonoff, CEO of Fit Energy. “We’re committed to being transparent, answering questions and building a long-term relationship with Newport Township as we move through the next stages of this project.”
—This content was contributed by the communications team for Fit Energy .

source_document.body:
For decades, procurement has been evaluated heavily on year-over-year Purchase Price Variance (PPV). Gartner identifies cost reduction, risk management , sustainability and innovation as procurement's leading value propositions—priorities that must increasingly be managed together rather than as competing mandates.
What’s Related
From a high-velocity technology supply chain perspective, the real question is not whether a more sustainable material or component carries a higher purchase price. The real question is: Does that option lower the total landed cost of delivering a good, verified unit to the customer? Once procurement measures this outcome, sustainability stops looking like an expensive corporate tax and starts functioning as rigorous operational discipline.
1. The mathematics of sourcing: Why the lowest bid is often the most expensive
A sourced component creates costs across every link of the supply chain long after the purchase order is signed: energy and raw material conversion, packaging tare weight, container cube utilization, transit demurrage, buffer inventory holding, quality inspection, line fallout, scrap handling, warranty returns, and end-of-life disposal liabilities.
Consider an illustrative electronics scenario: a mechanical subassembly carries a 5.0% unit discount, but also creates 3.5% factory fallout, requires 18% more packaging volume and adds 21 days of transit lead time. Once quality loss, packaging, freight and inventory are included, the apparent savings can disappear. These figures are an author-created illustration—not an industry benchmark—and demonstrate the total-cost-of-ownership logic recommended by the U.S. EPA.
Quantified areas where sustainable sourcing and cost optimization intersect:
Network Design & Co-location: An MIT CTL case study found that a supplier-park model could reduce total costs by 45%, improve speed to market by 30% and reduce transportation -related Scope 3 emissions by 82%. The result is case-specific, but it demonstrates why cost and carbon should be optimized together.
Material Yield & Packaging Productivity: Improving first-pass yield, reducing scrap, eliminating unnecessary void fill and increasing pallet or container utilization can lower material, handling and freight costs simultaneously. The business case should use measured supplier data rather than generic savings assumptions.
Regionalized Logistics : Shorter, simpler logistics lanes can reduce emissions, lead-time variability and in-transit inventory. The economics depend on labor , duties, capacity, service levels and demand—not distance alone.
Product Durability & Recovery: Designing for durability, repair, reuse and remanufacturing keeps products and materials in circulation, preserving embedded value while reducing returns and replacement demand.

2. The counter-theory: When sustainable sourcing actually drives costs up
A rigorous procurement framework must also consider the counterargument: sustainable sourcing doesn't automatically yield savings, and weak execution can erode operating margins. Industry research consistently highlights data quality, supplier engagement and implementation capability as central challenges.
Piu Ghosh
The Green Premium: Some low-carbon materials and processes still cost more. The World Economic Forum and Boston Consulting Group estimate that net-zero supply chains could raise end-consumer costs by 1% to 4% in the medium term, even while about 40% of emissions in the supply chains studied could be abated with readily available, affordable measures.
Broken Circular Logistics Loops: Reusable transport packaging can become uneconomic when return frequency is low, reverse freight is expensive or containers are lost. Circularity creates value only when products and materials remain in use through reliable maintenance, reuse, refurbishment, remanufacturing or recycling loops.
Capacity Inflexibility & Single-Source Premiums: Restricting an approved vendor list to a narrow set of certified suppliers can create concentration risk, capacity bottlenecks and costly expedites during demand surges.
Unstaged Capital Exposure: Large commitments to unproven materials, tooling or processes can create write-down risk when performance or demand fails to scale. Pilots and staged commitments should precede full allocation.
The economic lesson is clear: a green label earns zero commercial credit on its own. Sustainable sourcing lowers costs only when it meets the same rigorous yield, unit economics and risk hurdles applied to core manufacturing operations.
3. My proposed decision model: Operationalizing TRUE Cost
To bridge commercial negotiations, engineering feasibility and sustainability goals, I propose the four-part TRUE Cost model as a practical framework for evaluating direct sourcing decisions. In this model, TRUE represents Total Economics, Resource Productivity, Uncertainty and Resilience , and End-of-Life Value. The category weights, ranges and KPI thresholds shown below are my proposed starting points—not published industry benchmarks—and should be calibrated to each sourcing category. The model's total-cost logic aligns with EPA and DOE lifecycle-cost guidance.
Application and Scoring Methodology:
I developed the TRUE Cost scoring scale, KPI set and financial hurdle rates as adaptable decision aids rather than universal benchmarks. As an example, I propose scoring each bid from 1.0 (fails threshold) to 5.0 (leading performance) across 12 quantitative KPIs, followed by a financial gate such as positive NPV within an 18-to-24-month horizon or a minimum 15% IRR. Each company should calibrate these assumptions to its category, cost of capital and risk appetite.
4. Four levers that deliver dual economic and environmental value
Across multi-tier technology and industrial manufacturing networks, four strategic levers consistently unlock both cost reductions and Scope 3 emission cuts:
Specification Redesign & Value Engineering: Collaborate with R&D to eliminate non-functional over-engineering. Relaxing tolerances where product performance permits can reduce machining time, tool wear, energy consumption and scrap. Validate any benefit through engineering trials before changing specifications.
Deep-Tier Resource Productivity Audits: Require Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers to provide primary machine-level data, including energy per unit, scrap rates and water consumption, under steady-state operating conditions. Use the data to identify idle energy, low-yield steps and reclaimable material.
Supplier Collaboration & Gain-Sharing Agreements: Replace zero-sum reverse auctions with structured gain-sharing where appropriate. Buyers and suppliers can jointly optimize mold layouts, eliminate process steps or lightweight shipping fixtures, then share savings that are measured against an agreed baseline.
Closed-Loop Circularity & Scrap Reharvesting: Establish buyback or closed-loop contracts in which process scrap is returned to qualified recyclers or material producers for secondary raw-material credits, reducing disposal cost and exposure to virgin commodity markets.
5. Rewriting the procurement scorecard and commercial agreement
A procurement organization cannot execute a sustainable sourcing strategy if category managers are rewarded entirely on immediate Purchase Price Variance (PPV). When incentives prioritize short-term unit discounts, buyers naturally shift expenses into logistics buffers, factory rework and scrap liabilities.
Rebalance Buyer Performance Scorecards: As an illustrative application of the TRUE Cost model, I propose allocating 40% to total landed cost per good unit, 25% to resource productivity and scrap reduction, 20% to lead-time resilience and 15% to circular recovery milestones. These starting weights should vary by category strategy.
Contract for Auditable Data & Gain-Sharing: Master Service Agreements (MSAs) must require verified quarterly reporting on yield, energy intensity, and scrap reclamation, with explicit commercial bonuses tied to achieving mutual efficiency targets.
Staged Volume Commitments & Risk Gates: I also propose a staged transition for unproven sustainable alternatives: begin with a 5% pilot, move to a 25% validation ramp after yield targets are met, and reach full allocation only after commercial and operational performance is proven. These percentages illustrate the approach; they are not universal thresholds.
6. The new sourcing paradigm
The legacy procurement question was: 'What is the lowest unit price that satisfies the minimum engineering drawing?'
The Strategic Imperative: The modern procurement question must be: 'Which end-to-end sourcing configuration delivers the required customer outcome with the lowest total lifetime cost, lowest resource consumption, and lowest operational risk?'
Having managed global supply-chain operations across Amazon and Apple , I have observed firsthand why this paradigm shift is essential: technology product life cycles move quickly, supply chains span many multi-tier nodes, and decisions optimized in functional isolation can create costly operational drag elsewhere. source_document.body:
Uber Technologies is making a $2.3 billion bet on business-to-business food delivery with its acquisition of ezCater, a workplace catering platform whose orders average more than $400.
Uber announced Tuesday that it has agreed to acquire Boston-based ezCater in an all-cash transaction that will combine the company’s workplace catering business with Uber Eats and Uber for Business.
The deal gives Uber access to a large pool of higher-value, scheduled deliveries generated by corporate meetings, employee meal programs and events, according to a news release.
EzCater generated more than $2.5 billion in gross bookings during the trailing 12 months, growing in the high teens year over year. The company is profitable on a non-GAAP operating income basis and is expected to be margin accretive to Uber. Its average order value exceeds $400.
The platform allows businesses to order from more than 140,000 restaurants nationwide and provides tools for companies to manage ordering and food spending.
For Uber (NYSE: UBER ), the acquisition provides another way to put commercial delivery volume through its existing network while expanding its B2B business.
The company said restaurants could gain access to larger orders and new customers, while Uber Eats couriers would have additional opportunities to earn from catering deliveries.
“Catering is a big business, and can be a huge revenue stream for restaurants,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in announcing the transaction.
EzCater CEO Nihad Rahman said combining the company’s catering and B2B expertise with Uber would provide access to Uber’s broader network of customers, merchants and couriers.
The acquisition is expected to close in the coming months, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.
Uber Freight adds implementation executive
Separately, Uber Freight announced Monday that Erin Mitchell has joined the Chicago-based company as senior vice president of implementation.
Erin Mitchell
Mitchell will lead customer onboarding for Uber Freight’s Transportation Management business, including helping customers implement its transportation management system .
Mitchell previously served as chief operating officer at YMX Logistics and held an executive position at Kraft Heinz, giving her experience on both the logistics provider and corporate supply chain sides of the industry.
“Transportation touches so much of a company’s business—from warehouse costs and service levels to its ability to grow,” Mitchell said in a statement. “I’ve led supply chain operations and been responsible for delivering logistics services, so I understand both what customers expect and what it takes to deliver consistently.
Why it matters: The ezCater deal expands Uber’s reach into higher-value business deliveries while Mitchell’s appointment underscores Uber Freight’s focus on converting transportation technology sales into successful customer deployments.

Tesla has turned on Powershare Home Backup for the Model 3 and Model Y, which means its two volume cars can now send power back into a house during an outage. Until today, the Cybertruck was the only Tesla that could do it.
There are limits. You need a Powerwall 3, and Tesla only guarantees the feature on cars ordered since October 1. Ford and GM have been selling EVs that can back up a home for years.
What Tesla announced
Tesla Energy announced the launch on X today:
Powershare Home Backup is now available for new Model 3 & Model Y with Powerwall 3 Extend your home backup by over 2 days with your vehicle pic.twitter.com/a0codvZ2yH — Tesla Energy (@teslaenergy) October 6, 2026
Tesla’s updated Powershare page says the feature is “currently available for all Cybertruck vehicles, and all new Model 3 and Model Y vehicles ordered on October 1, 2026 or later.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Here’s how it works. You plug the car into a Wall Connector or Universal Wall Connector at a home that has a Powerwall 3. When the grid goes down, the car’s battery pack extends your backup.
Tesla says a Model 3 or Model Y adds “over two days” of backup for a home that uses 30 kWh a day, starting from a 90% charge. Standard trims get “up to two days.” A Cybertruck adds more than three. Tesla lists a maximum continuous output of 11.52 kW for the Powerwall setup.
If you already have a Powerwall 3 and a Wall Connector, Tesla says you don’t need any extra hardware. But you do have to contact Tesla support to get it turned on.
It’s a big change from two months ago. In August, Tesla added a 2.4 kW outlet adapter to the Model Y Premium , and its website still said Powershare was “not available” for the Model 3 and Model Y. Last month, Cybertruck’s Powershare started working with Powerwall 3 after repeated delays.
The fine print
The word “new” matters in that announcement.
Tesla’s footnote says the guarantee covers cars ordered in the US and Puerto Rico after October 1. For anything built before that, Tesla says “some, but not all” Model 3 and Model Y vehicles have the capability.
It comes down to hardware. Tesla says bidirectional power on the Model 3 and Model Y runs through an inverter it calls PCS2 Lite, and it hasn’t said when that part went into production on each trim. Owners can check on the touchscreen under Software, then Additional Vehicle Information. If “Powershare Support” is enabled, the car has it.
And there are more limits:
Powerwall 3 is required. Tesla says Powerwall 2 and Powerwall+ support is “coming soon.”
No Powerwall, no home backup. Cybertruck owners can use a Powershare Gateway instead, but Tesla doesn’t offer that option for Model 3 and Model Y.
You can’t sell power back to the grid. Tesla says Grid Support is “not available for Model 3 or Model Y.”
Model S and Model X aren’t included.
It’s US and Puerto Rico only. Tesla’s Canadian site still lists Powershare as a Cybertruck-only feature.
Tesla is late to this
Ford launched home backup on the F-150 Lightning in 2022 with 9.6 kW of output. That’s four years ago.
GM committed in 2023 to bring vehicle-to-home to every Ultium-based EV by model year 2026 , and it delivered. GM Energy’s compatibility list now includes the Equinox EV, Blazer EV, Silverado EV, the 2027 Bolt, GMC’s Sierra EV and Hummer EV, and five Cadillacs. Kia offers it on the EV9 through a Wallbox bidirectional charger, and we keep a running list of EVs that can power a home .
Tesla set its own deadline and missed it. At Investor Day in March 2023, Drew Baglino, then Tesla’s SVP of powertrain and energy engineering, said bidirectional charging could come “within the next two years.” That pointed to 2025.
At the same event, Elon Musk said: “I don’t think very many people are going to want to use bidirectional charging, unless you have a Powerwall.” Three and a half years later, that’s exactly how Tesla shipped it.
And a third party got there first. Last year, we reported that Sigenergy’s home battery system could do vehicle-to-home with Tesla vehicles over DC, without Tesla’s involvement.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla is playing catch-up here. Ford did this in 2022, and GM has it across its EV lineup. Tesla sells the cars, the chargers, and the home batteries, and it’s getting to it in late 2026. It is also attaching the feature to Powerwall 3, which clearly explains why Tesla didn’t want to do vehicle-to-home before: it didn’t want to cannibalize the Powerwall.
But better late than never. And there’s a lot to like.

Mitsubishi is taking another crack at the US EV market, nearly a decade after it stopped selling the i-MiEV in 2017.
The new 2027 Eclipse Sportback EV will go on sale this month priced from $37,745, Mitsubishi said on Tuesday. With the $1,995 destination fee, prices come to $39,740.
Already “exceptionally well equipped,” it will be available with one optional upgrade: the Technology Package, which adds $2,600.

Mitsubishi’s new EV is essentially a rebadged Nissan LEAF. As part of the Japanese automakers’ alliance, the Mitsubishi Eclipse Sportback EV is based on the same platform as the LEAF and uses the same 75 kWh liquid-cooled battery.
So how do they stack up? The Eclipse Sportback EV offers an EPA-estimated range of up to 282 miles, compared to the base Nissan Leaf S+, which offers up to 303 miles.
2027 Mitsubishi Eclipse Sportback EV at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Mitsubishi)
All Nissan LEAF models use the same 75 kWh battery, but the EPA range drops to 259 miles on the top Platinum+ trim. The highest-priced Nissan LEAF Platinum+ starts at $38,990, while the mid-grade SV+ trim is priced from $34,230.
Like the LEAF, Mitsubishi’s EV comes with a native NACS port so that you can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter.
With DC fast charging of up to 150 kW, the Mitsubishi Eclipse Sportback EV can recharge from 10% to 80% in around 35 minutes. That’s the same as the Leaf.
2027 Mitsubishi Eclipse Sportback EV interior (Source: Mitsubishi)
Although it shares the same underpinnings, Mitsubishi promises the new EV will stand out with the brand’s unique style. It’s similar to Toyota and Subaru’s alliance.
It’s about the same shape and size as the Leaf, but the Eclipse EV features Mitsubishi’s logo and Triple Diamond design.
Inside, Mitsubishi’s EV features an all-black synthetic leather interior and dual 14.3″ digital driver displays with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. The setup includes built-in Google with Intelligent Route Planning powered by Google Maps.
2027 Mitsubishi Eclipse Sportback EV interior (Source: Mitsubishi)
In comparison, the base Nissan LEAF S+ has dual 12.3″ displays. The higher-priced SV+ and Platinum+ have dual 14.3″ displays.
The new EV is the first from Mitsubishi’s new North American business plan, Momentum 2030. Mitsubishi plans to launch at least one new or refreshed vehicle each year through fiscal 2030.
Following the Eclipse Sportback EV, the new Outlander SUV will debut, followed by several “adventure-oriented and off-road capable vehicles,” Mitsubishi said.

Starting at nearly $40,000, including the destination fee, Mitsubishi’s new Eclipse Sportback EV might be a tough sell.
For one, it’s already about $8,000 more than its twin, the LEAF. It’s also more than many current top-selling EVs, including the Hyundai IONIQ 5 ($35,250) and Toyota bZ ($34,980).
It’s also about $8,000 more than the new 2027 Kia EV3 ( see our review ), which offers up to 321 miles of EPA range.
The base EV3 Light trim starts at $29,890 and uses a 58.3 kWh battery with up to 221 miles of range.
Upgrading to the Kia EV3 Wind, which uses an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range, is still cheaper, priced from $34,990.

ShipStation has launched Ship with Walmart, giving Walmart Marketplace sellers access to Walmart-negotiated shipping rates and seller protections directly within its shipping platform. The service is available to ShipStation users and currently covers U.S. domestic shipments only.
What’s Related
Sellers can activate Ship with Walmart, buy eligible shipping labels and manage Walmart Marketplace orders through their existing ShipStation account. It works alongside their existing carrier accounts as another shipping option, with no new integration to build.
The integration also includes up to $100 in protection for eligible lost-item claims on orders shipped on time. Walmart Marketplace orders appear alongside orders from Amazon , TikTok Shop, Shopify, eBay and other connected storefronts, allowing sellers to manage shipping from the same dashboard.
“Sellers shouldn't have to choose between the tools they rely on every day and the benefits their marketplace offers them,” said Matt Norman, vice president of strategic business development at ShipStation. “Ship with Walmart closes that gap. Sellers get Walmart-negotiated rates and seller protections, including up to $100 of order protection, all within the ShipStation platform.”
RELATED STORIES: Walmart to Convert Vacant Retail Space Into Delivery Depots | ShipStation Adds LTL Freight Shipping to Its Parcel Platform
Shipping benefits easy to access
Ship with Walmart gives sellers access to discounted rates from domestic carriers. After activation, they can purchase eligible labels directly in ShipStation while continuing to use their other shipping accounts.
For sellers handling orders from several marketplaces, the integration puts Walmart’s shipping benefits inside the software they already use to process orders. They can manage Walmart shipments alongside their other sales channels without leaving ShipStation.
The announcement does not identify participating carriers or specify the size of the label discounts. It also does not compare these rates with those available through sellers’ existing carrier accounts.
Protection for lost-package claims
The lost-package protection covers eligible claims for packages lost in transit or after delivery , provided the orders were shipped on time. Sellers can also access negative feedback reviews for approved lost-item claims.
ShipStation says Ship with Walmart supports on-time delivery and valid tracking performance. Those features accompany the discounted labels and claim protections, though the announcement does not detail every eligibility requirement.
Carrier recommendations and a subscription offer
The integration also brings Walmart’s Simplified Shipping Settings into ShipStation. The feature displays Walmart-recommended carriers and shipping service options based on the delivery promise the seller has made to the customer.
Walmart Marketplace sellers new to ShipStation can receive 20% off their ShipStation subscription for one year when they activate Ship with Walmart. The subscription offer can be combined with discounted label rates, subject to eligibility requirements and offer terms.

source_document.body:
Trade associations representing chemical manufacturers — whose supply chains are dependent on railroads — have been among the most outspoken critics of the proposed Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern merger.
But this week the largest producer of polyvinyl chloride in the U.S. told federal regulators that it supports the transcontinental merger.
“As a solely served customer, Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP ) transports 100% of our rail traffic from each of our three production locations,” Shintech President Yasuhikoh Saitoh wrote in a letter to the Surface Transportation Board . “We rely on them to transport our products safely, reliably, and efficiently and we also depend on them to provide competitive pricing that allows us to win business both domestically and globally so that we can continue to grow.”
Saitoh praised UP for investing in its Gulf Coast carload network, including expanded storage-in-transit yards near its plants in Louisiana and Texas, and said the merged railroad’s ability to provide single-line service to eastern destinations would be an advantage.
“The proposed Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern ( NYSE: NSC ) merger is very important to us. The eastern U.S. is one of our largest destination markets and we are enthusiastic about the synergies to be gained through reaching those markets on a single railroad,” Saitoh wrote. “A single line railroad will increase speed, reduce costs, enhance competition and improve the United States supply chain. Union Pacific has a history of consistently providing transportation solutions that enhance our competitiveness and support continued investment in our business.”
The Houston-based company is the U.S. arm of Japanese chemical producer Shin-Etsu. It has plants in Plaquemine and Addis, La., and Freeport, Texas. The PVC the company produces is used in a range of products, including pipes, flooring, medical devices, and packaging.
Concerns for short lines
Separately, a longtime railroad executive told the STB that the combined UP-NS system would have a negative impact on the short line railroads that have been driving growth in carload traffic.
The merger “poses serious harm for short lines and their rail customers” because an expanded UP would possess too much market power, George Avery Grimes told the board in a 23-page filing .
He urged the board to eliminate “artificial market barriers,” including paper barriers and handling agreements that limit short line interchange options, and to adopt a reasonable service standard.
“UP’s filings in this docket suggest increased density and capacity constraints, and its asymmetry of power extends to the competition for capacity between high-priority PSR operations and lower-priority local services. A reasonable service standard designed by the Board would help anchor the definition of Enhanced Competition, balance shipper needs with the realities of railroad operations, and ensure that banished artificial market levers cannot return in the form of service penalties for shippers served by short lines interchanging with an integrated post-merger UP,” Grimes wrote.
Grimes, who worked at Missouri Pacific, Union Pacific, and Kansas City Southern and held positions at short line holding companies OmniTRAX and Patriot Rail, holds a doctorate in railroad engineering, economics, and finance.

Spot container freight rates from Asia to the United States have likely reached their post-Hormuz crisis peak, but shippers should expect elevated costs through the remainder of 2026, according to Xeneta Chief Analyst Peter Sand.
Market-average spot rates edged higher Oct. 1, reaching $8,346 per forty-foot equivalent unit to the U.S. West Coast and $11,523 per FEU to the East Coast. Those increases of 1.4% and 0.7%, respectively, from Sept. 24 left rates more than four times their Feb. 28 pre-crisis levels.
“Spot rates from Far East to the U.S. ticked up again on October 1, but we can say with a level of confidence that the market has reached its post-Hormuz crisis peak in 2026,” Sand said.
Easing port congestion in Asia as typhoon season winds down is helping turn the market, he said. China’s Golden Week and national holidays are also reducing exports during the first week of October.
“Demand is not strong and rates have now peaked, but they will not collapse, so shippers should expect to pay elevated freight costs for the remainder of the year,” Sand said.
Xeneta expects a steeper decline on the Asia–U.S. East Coast trade than on the West Coast route, reflecting the East Coast’s higher starting point. East Coast rates stood $3,177 per FEU above West Coast rates Oct. 1, compared with a $772 premium before the Hormuz crisis.
Sand expects that gap to narrow as rates retreat through the rest of the year. Looking ahead three months, he forecast East Coast spot rates in a range of $6,000 to $7,000 per FEU and West Coast rates around $4,500 to $5,500.
“That would be a sizable correction, but not a collapse,” he said.
The anticipated turn in U.S.-bound rates follows an earlier reversal on routes from the Far East to Europe. Sand said rates to North Europe and the Mediterranean peaked much earlier and have been falling since the beginning of July.
Asia–North Europe spot rates declined 2.1% in the latest week to $3,726 per FEU, while Mediterranean rates fell 4.6% to $4,105. Despite those declines, rates remained 67.9% and 23.3% above their respective pre-crisis levels.
On the North Europe–U.S. East Coast trade, rates fell 2.2% week over week to $2,893 per FEU, still 95.9% above the Feb. 28 baseline.
Sand cautioned that the outlook remains vulnerable.
“We can also not discount further major disruptions or geopolitic conflict that would change the situation dramatically once again,” he said.

source_document.body:
Transportation prices continued to surge in September as capacity tightened further, according to a monthly sentiment survey of supply chain executives.
The Logistics Managers’ Index showed transportation prices (92.7) remained highly inflationary, up 2.7 percentage points from August . (The LMI is a diffusion index in which a reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below 50 signals contraction.)
The pricing index has logged readings of 90 or above in five of the past six months. Record diesel fuel prices and heightened regulatory enforcement continue to restrict truck capacity, keeping the index near all-time highs.
Transportation capacity (34.4) experienced “a steep rate of contraction,” falling 5.6 points sequentially. The dataset has signaled contraction for 10 straight months. Transportation utilization (66.1) increased notably, but at a rate that was 4.5 points slower than in the prior month.
Logistics managers surveyed expect the transportation market to remain very tight over the next 12 months, returning future readings of 37.9 for capacity, 70.8 for utilization and 86.1 for pricing.
SONAR: Outbound Tender Rejection Index (OTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
SONAR: Van Contract Rate Per Mile Index ( VCRPM1.USA ) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). The index shows a 7-day moving average of the initial reporting of dry van contract rates without fuel or accessorial charges.
The overall LMI (70.2) was up 3.6 points in September to the second-highest level in four and a half years. (June’s 71.1 reading was the highest level recorded over that period.)
Inventory levels (58.9) increased 6.1 points, keeping inventory costs elevated at 79.9, 1.3 points above August.
The report said retail inventories are still sitting at the wholesale level of the supply chain. Upstream respondents (wholesalers and manufacturers) returned a 61.4 reading for inventory levels, while downstream respondents (mostly retailers) returned a 53.8 reading.
“This dynamic likely represents a combination of goods being rushed over late due to late-breaking confidence in Q4 consumer spending along with the neo-seasonal trend to only move goods down to retailers in mid-October,” the Tuesday report said.
“This increase likely reflects two things: first, inventories were not overbuilt in summer 2026 to avoid tariffs; second, U.S. consumers have remained strong in the face of inflationary pressures and retailers are building stocks accordingly.”
It also noted that companies have not “finished building up inventories” ahead of the holidays.
Increased inventories pushed warehouse capacity (39.3) 14.2 points lower and into contraction territory. This was the fastest rate of contraction for warehousing space since March 2022, shortly after Russia’s initial invasion of Ukraine. Warehouse capacity was nearly 10 points tighter upstream, where the bulk of the inventories sit.
Warehousing utilization (64.3) increased 4.7 points, with warehouse prices (73.5) continuing to see “robust expansion,” but down 1.5 points sequentially.
Aggregate logistics costs (inventory, warehousing and transportation) totaled 246.1 during the month, up 2.5 points sequentially.
“This is the highest reading for this aggregate metric since April of 2022, when supply-driven inflation was rampant in the wake of both the cessation of COVID-era demand and the invasion of Ukraine,” the report said. “These high costs are putting significant pressure on supply chains and consumers alike.”
The LMI is a collaboration among Arizona State University, Colorado State University, Florida Atlantic University, Rutgers University and the University of Nevada, Reno, conducted with the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals.
Why it matters? The Logistics Managers’ Index provides a look at all major supply chain costs. The latest report signals a difficult operating environment for shippers characterized by limited capacity and rising costs.

A stack of 155mm artillery rounds sit behind the line of AS90 self propelled guns and their Ukrainian operators (UK MoD)
SINGAPORE – Australia’s efforts to develop its sovereign guided weapons manufacturing continue to make progress but risks remain, with two think tanks this year calling for the country to further diversify its sources and take concrete steps to ensure its workforce is in place to support its plans.
The Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance (GWEO), Canberra’s effort to create domestic production for guided missiles, was launched in 2024. According to its 2026 National Defence Strategy (NDS), Australia plans to set aside between 26 and 36 billion Australian dollars ($18.16 to $25.14 billion) in funding for the GWEO, although the NDS and accompanying integrated investment plan did not contain a lot of details into where the funding will be allocated.
So far, the effort has four official partners: the Australian arms of Norwegian firm Kongsberg, French company Thales, and US giants Lockheed Martin, Raytheon. There are also two local companies tapped as “Enterprise and Support Partners” for the program.
The plan has already hit a few milestones, with Australia having test fired locally produced Lockheed’s Guided Multiple Launched Rocket Systems (GMLRS) rockets, found local industry partners to produce GMLRS components, and entered an agreement to develop and produce Precision Strike Missiles.
It will also become the first export customer for the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM) after having developed and tested the munition . It will also locally manufacture Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile and Joint Strike Missile.
The latter two milestones are noteworthy, as the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) noted in April that a large proportion of the munitions being produced under the GWEO are American in origin and that US manufacturers are already struggling to meet demand.
The think tank echoed Australia’s NDS in supporting Australia’s efforts to diversify its sources of munitions, noting that “South Korea, Britain and Germany offer credible technology transfer pathways for components and complete weapons that could reduce dependence.”
Another Australian think tank also cautioned that workforce shortages in Australia presents an additional risk to the GWEO effort, and called on the Australian government to take the lead in heading off the issue.
The United States Studies Centre (USSC) at the University of Sydney called Australia’s current industrial workforce planning “largely neglected” in a June report , and called on the Australian government to “address current trends of deferred responsibility, ambiguous demand signals and ad hoc, incremental coordination across industry, state governments and training providers to ensure the success of the GWEO enterprise.”
Noting that Australia’s technical workforce tended to be geographically immobile due to “preference and circumstance,” planning for the siting of GWEO facilities needed to be decided quicker and better coordinated among Australia’s state and federal governments.
“To succeed, there must be moves beyond ad hoc coordination and clear, long-term demand signals necessary to attract and train the specialised talent required for this mission,” said USSC Director of Foreign Policy and Defence Lavina Lee in the report.
Nevertheless, ASPI was upbeat on the program, noting that it “has been hitting milestones on the way to closing capability gaps and building domestic industrial foundations.”
Similarly, the former head of Australia’s GWEO Group, Air Marshal Leon Phillips, said he was proud of what the organization, which has been tasked with overseeing the program, has achieved.
“We’ve focused on deepening our war stocks, enhancing our lethality and reach – particularly long-range strike – and importantly, building domestic manufacturing capability,” he said prior to leaving the post in September.
Continued Expansion
The latest milestone for GWEO actually came today during the Land Forces exhibition in Perth, with the announcement that Kongsberg Australia has signed an Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Zone 5 Technologies for manufacturing guided missiles.
Both companies will “explore collaboration opportunities to provide affordable, mass producible long-range strike and air-defence and anti-drone missiles for Australia and New Zealand,” per a release.
Kongsberg, who concluded its acquisition of Zone 5 in June, says that the MoU “establishes a framework for the organisations to collaborate on local manufacturing and supply chain opportunities and builds on Kongsberg’s growing weapons manufacturing capability in Australia.”
John Fry, Kongsberg Australia’s managing director, said that current events in the US and Europe show that “the ability to produce capable and affordable effectors quickly and at scale” was required.
“Building resilient supply chains and industrial capacity is critical to ensuring Australia and its allies can sustain capability when it matters. Key design principles for Zone 5 Technologies’ solutions are simplified supply chains and manufacturability at scale,” he said.
Zone 5 produces the AGM-188 Rusty Dagger long-range strike missile that has reportedly been used by Ukraine as well as the White Spike counter-drone air defense missile.

A worker on the Cordero silver project site. Credit: Discovery Mining.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 6, 2026
Discovery Mining (TSX: DSV, US-OTC: DSVSF) said it received two key environmental and land-use permits from the Mexican government, allowing the Canadian miner to advance its Cordero silver project toward development.
Mexico’s environmental department, SEMARNAT, approved Cordero’s environmental impact assessment and Change of Land Use permit, completing the project’s federal environmental approval process, Discovery said Monday in a statement . Discovery still needs to complete development planning and financing before construction can begin.
Toronto-based Discovery has been updating Cordero’s February 2024 feasibility study to reflect current capital and operating costs. It’s also evaluating whether natural gas or grid power should be the main source of electricity, in addition to working with water-treatment plant operators on an upgrade to the local facility.
Receipt of federal permits “is a major milestone, and while Cordero is not yet fully construction ready, it should now earn a higher multiple and lower jurisdictional discount,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Rabi Nizami said Tuesday in a note.
“The longer-term path to realize full value from Cordero can now be better evaluated, as the project becomes more financeable and strategically valuable for Discovery, with greater optionality for a joint venture, strategic investment, outright sale or asset-level financing arrangement if the company elects to build.”
Permits expected
Other analysts were similarly positive, though SCP Resource Finance noted the approval had become increasingly expected as Mexico began moving more mining permits through the system.
Cordero’s approval was significant because of the project’s scale and showed that large greenfield open-pit projects with existing concessions can still advance under the current administration, SCP said. The firm raised its Discovery price target by $1.20 to C$13.80 after increasing the multiple it applies to Cordero.
BMO Capital Markets analyst Kevin O’Halloran called the permits the final major hurdle for Cordero and said no further major approvals are required before development. BMO models first production in the second half of 2029 and values Cordero at $2.73 billion using a long-term silver price of $47 per oz. It rates Discovery outperform with a C$16 target.
Scotiabank, which carries Cordero at about C$3.4 billion, or 32% of its asset value estimate, said an updated feasibility study using current metals prices could show “meaningful upside” to the project’s economics.
Large reserves
Discovery acquired Cordero in 2019 and has since invested more than $100 million (C$140 million) in exploration and technical work on the project. The 2024 feasibility study outlined a 19-year mine producing an average of 37 million oz. of silver equivalent annually during its first 12 years. It estimated average all-in sustaining costs below $12.50 per silver-equivalent oz. during the first eight years.
Located in the northern part of Mexico’s Central Mexican Silver Belt, a prolific mining region in Chihuahua state, Cordero ranks among the world’s largest undeveloped silver reserves.
It holds 327 million proven and probable tonnes grading 29 grams silver per tonne, 0.08 gram gold, 0.41% lead and 0.72% zinc for contained metal of 302 million oz. silver, 840,000 oz. gold, 3 billion lb. lead and 5.2 billion lb. zinc, according to a February 2024 resource.
About 240 million tonnes of measured and indicated resources lie outside the pit used in the feasibility study, providing potential for future mine-life expansion, Discovery says.
Using a silver price of $22 per oz., Discovery estimated initial capital costs of $606 million and an after-tax net present value of $1.2 billion.
Discovery shares fell 2.3% to C$11.92 in Tuesday morning in Toronto as investors took profits following the widely anticipated permit approvals. The stock has nearly tripled over the past year and recently traded as high as C$13.43. The company has a market capitalization of C$9.7 billion ($6.8 billion).

AbbVie and Genmab’s bispecific antibody blew analyst expectations out of the water with a 51% improvement in progression-free survival when used alongside a standard frontline regimen in diffuse large B cell lymphoma—potentially setting up a battle with Roche’s Polivy.
When used in the frontline setting on top of a common anti-cancer regimen, AbbVie and Genmab’s Epkinly cut the risk of disease progression or death by more than half in patients with newly diagnosed diffuse large B cell lymphoma—besting the results of Roche’s Polivy and potentially positioning the drug as “the new standard of care” in this indication, according to William Blair.
The progression-free survival (PFS) benefit seen with Epkinly, already approved for later lines of treatment in diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), is the strongest treatment effect disclosed among major registrational trials in frontline treatment of the cancer, the analysts wrote wrote in a Monday afternoon note to investors. The readout “knocks it out of the park,” they said.
The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial , which enrolled 900 patients , is the first Phase 3 study of a bispecific antibody combination therapy to show statistically significant improvement, AbbVie and Genmab said in a press release on Monday .
Compared with treatment with only R-CHOP—a five-drug regimen based on Roche’s rituximab—the Epkinly-based combo led to a 51% reduction in the risk of disease progression or death, AbbVie and Genmab reported Monday. Not only did the result hit the study’s primary endpoint, it greatly exceeded analyst expectations of a 30–35% benefit. This PFS benefit was the same for patients with high-risk and low- to intermediate-risk disease.
“We view the result as highly differentiated and squarely within our best-case scenario, ” Truist Securities analysts wrote to investors on Monday.
As for safety, the companies noted that using Epkinly with R-CHOP was generally well-tolerated, with side effects consistent with what is known for the individual drugs.
Genmab shares popped nearly 11% at close of trading to $38.48 following the data reveal.
The company originally partnered with AbbVie in 2020 to collaborate on the development of Epkinly , a CD20xCD3 bispecific T cell engager, that was first approved in May 2023 for patients with for DLBCL who have undergone at least two prior lines of systemic treatment. If greenlit in the first-line setting, Epkinly will compete with Roche’s Polivy and potentially Incyte’s Monjuvi.
AbbVie and Genmab plan to bring the new data to global regulatory authorities to determine the next steps for the investigational combo. The partners also plan to present a more complete analysis of EPCORE DLBCL-2 at an upcoming medical meeting.
Epkinly’s Phase 3 results compare favorably to benchmarks set by existing treatment regimens based on Monjuvi and Polivy, William Blair said.
Polivy was approved by the FDA for first-line DLBCL in April 2023 after the drug, combined with a modified version of R-CHOP reduced the risk of disease progression, relapse or death by 27% in a Phase 3 trial .
Monjuvi plus R-CHOP, meanwhile, hit 25% progression-free survival in a Phase 3 trial in January, meeting the study’s primary endpoint. Incyte indicated plans at the time to file for FDA approval in the indication in the first half of this year.
AbbVie and Genmab’s readout represents an “overwhelmingly positive improvement” in favor of the Epkinly combo, William Blair said, noting that the data significantly exceeded the firm’s base case scenario. The firm had originally anticipated a 35% PFS benefit. Truist, meanwhile, had expected the Epkinly regimen to cut the likelihood of disease progression or death by 30%.
Truist also emphasized the consistency of Epkinly’s ability to reduce disease progression across risk groups, a robust treatment effect the analysts “should support regulatory discussion across the broader population.
“While full data remain important for absolute benefit, durability, OS, and safety, the topline result supports a potentially practice-changing profile and a credible path toward a broad 1L label, in our view,” Truist continued.
The study is expected to wrap up in June 2027 , according to Clinicaltrials.gov.
Notably, Epkinly in January failed to improve survival in a separate Phase 3 study in patients with relapsed, refractory DLBCL who are ineligible for or for whom prior treatments have not worked, missing the trial’s primary endpoint.

Despite the late-stage miss, analysts maintained confidence in the Epkinly program, with Truist Securities saying the result “doesn’t waver our optimism” regarding the bispecific antibody’s ongoing frontline trial.

Despite the regulatory delay, Novo is still expecting a 2027 launch for its hemophilia A drug denecimig.
The FDA needs more time to review Novo’s investigational bispecific antibody for hemophilia A before making an approval decision, citing manufacturing issues as the reason behind the delay.
The agency said “ongoing facility remediation activities” were the reason for the extension, according to a release from Novo. The FDA did not identify any deficiencies related to the efficacy or safety of the drug, known as denecimig, according to the Danish pharma.
Novo submitted the next-gen factor VIII mimetic for FDA review in September 2025, with a decision slated for the third quarter of this year. Novo announced the agency’s delay on the second day of the fourth quarter.
The FDA has yet to share a new timeline for the review, according to Novo, which is working to address the agency’s remediation requests related to the unnamed manufacturing site.
The FDA’s manufacturing flag does not impact other marketed Novo products, the pharma said. Novo is still banking on FDA approval, saying the company is still preparing for a 2027 denecimig launch for hemophilia A in adults and children.
“Novo is already in the process of addressing the FDA’s requests as efficiently as possible and continuing to work closely with the Agency toward bringing denecimig to patients in the US,” Novo CEO Mike Doustdar said in a prepared statement.

Geologist looking at Beaver drill core. Credit: Inomin Mines
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 6, 2026
First-pass drilling at Inomin Mines’ (TSXV: MINE) Lynx block in central British Columbia cut 420 metres of near-surface nickel-magnesium mineralization, marking a second discovery area 10 km south of Beaver. Shares rose.
Hole L26-04 returned 0.21% total nickel and 22% magnesium over 420 metres from 3 metres downhole. L26-03 cut 392.5 metres grading 0.22% total nickel and 23.5% magnesium from 2.5 metres. The project lies 50 km north of Williams Lake and about 450 km north of Vancouver, near Trekor Metals’ (TSX, LSE: TKO; NYSE American: TGB) Gibraltar copper mine.
Asked whether the low nickel grades could support a mine, President and CEO John Gomez said the magnesium content could prove decisive.
“Obviously, we won’t know until there’s a feasibility study done on the project and market prices at the time,” Gomez told The Northern Miner by phone. “But the real kicker might be the magnesium. That is not low-grade. This is 20% to 25% magnesium.”
Inomin shares jumped more than a third on the discovery news to set a new 12-month high at 15¢ on Tuesday, after testing a low of 5¢ in the same period. The company has a market capitalization of $8 million (US$5.6 million).
Magnesium high
The discovery gives Japan’s Sumitomo Metal Mining (TSE: 5713) a second drilled area to assess under an option that could give it 80% of the project.
Sumitomo is funding exploration under an earn-in but hasn’t yet disclosed an ownership stake. It can earn 60% by spending $3 million by April 2027 and another 20% through a further $5-million investment. Inomin remains operator during the first phase.
All four holes reported Tuesday crossed between 330 and 420 metres of mineralization near the surface, Inomin said. The intervals are core lengths and true widths remain unknown. The holes were spaced at least 200 metres apart.
Target rich
Inomin drilled nine holes totalling 3,452.8 metres at Onuki, a 6-sq.-km magnetic target, and surveyed 158.4-line km with ground magnetics. Assays for five holes remain pending.
Onuki is one of seven magnetic targets across the 173 sq. km Lynx property. The targets generally extend for 1.5-3 km, but only Onuki has been drilled, Gomez said.
Inomin’s release said initial indications confirmed continuity between Lynx and Beaver, but Gomez said the 10-km gap hasn’t been tested.
“We don’t know yet,” he said. “We haven’t done any testing there. It’s really unknown what’s in between.”
Recovery test
The total-fusion assays measure nickel held in both sulphide and silicate minerals. Inomin hasn’t disclosed the sulphide-hosted share at Lynx, so the reported grades alone don’t show how much nickel flotation could recover.
In January, Inomin said Activation Laboratories had developed a partial-digestion assay to estimate sulphide nickel in samples grading more than 0.1% total nickel, but these rsults have not yet been released.
Earlier tests on a single eight-metre composite from Beaver recovered up to 58% of its nickel by flotation and extracted 99% of its magnesium using hydrochloric acid, according to Inomin.
Partner path
Sumitomo Metal Mining Canada funded the $2.3-million drilling program, as well as a$1.7-million program in 2025, bringing the two announced exploration budgets to $4 million. Inomin hasn’t said whether Sumitomo has formally exercised its 60% option.
Once the remaining Lynx assays arrive, the partners will consider step out and infill drilling at Beaver South, Gomez said. Enough drilling there could support a maiden resource in 2027.
“We’re just a small junior. We’re not going to be in production ourselves,” Gomez said. “We hope Sumitomo is the one that advances it all the way. They’re big enough. They’re capable of doing that.”

source_document.body:
Westwin Elements’ demonstration nickel refinery in Lawton, Oklahoma. Credit: Westwin Elements.
By: Staff Writer October 6, 2026
Westwin Elements plans to invest $502 million over five years to build a commercial-scale high-purity nickel refinery in Mississippi, as the U.S. seeks to expand domestic processing of critical minerals.
The Natchez project would annually produce 18,000 tonnes of high-purity nickel, known as Class 1, in its first stage, with commissioning targeted for 2029, the privately held company said Monday. Westwin has completed a bankable feasibility study and secured a long-term lease at the Belwood Industrial Site, about 145 km southwest of state capital Jackson.
The project would build on Westwin’s Lawton plant in Oklahoma, a 20-tonne-per-year demonstration operation that has completed multiple production runs of nickel powder using carbonyl refining technology, the company said. Lawton produces nickel powder with purity of at least 99.9%, Westwin says. Natchez would expand that process to commercial scale in the United States.
“Westwin was founded with the mission of delivering a win for the West and restoring the blue-collar American dream by bringing a critical industry back home,” CEO KaLeigh Long said in a news release. “The Natchez site gives us the capacity to produce American-made Class 1 nickel at scale, strengthening a critical domestic supply our country needs while creating high-paying careers.”
Financing ahead
Westwin said last month it had raised or secured $100 million since its founding in 2022 through equity, convertible instruments and other financing backed by private investors and family offices.
It has also signed $1.7 billion in binding, multiyear sales agreements, the company added. Those include a seven-year agreement with metals trader Traxys covering 10,000 tonnes of high-purity nickel briquettes annually and another sales agreement covering nickel powder and briquettes.
Binding feedstock and offtake agreements are in place to support the first stage of production at Natchez, Westwin said. The company is continuing work on financing, engineering and site development as it moves towards commercial-scale production.
The Belwood site is near Natchez’s inland port on the Mississippi River and has access to regional transportation networks. Westwin expects the first stage to create 134 full-time jobs paying an average of about $84,000 annually.
Nickel is on the U.S. critical-minerals list and is used in high-strength steel and rechargeable batteries. High-purity nickel is also used in aerospace, defence, specialty alloys and advanced manufacturing.

With its acquisition of IntraBio, Shionogi will gain ownership over Aqneursa, which could hit peak global sales of $1 billion across its two indications in Niemann-Pick disease type C and ataxia-telangiectasia, according to Jefferies.
Shionogi has moved to acquire commercial-stage IntraBio for $2 billion upfront just weeks after the Texas-based biotech secured an FDA approval in a rare disease for which there are no other treatments.
The centerpiece of the deal is IntraBio’s Aqneursa, which the FDA cleared in September 2024 for Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC), an ultrarare, progressive genetic disorder that impacts lysosomal storage and can cause life-threatening complications. There are around 1,000 potential patients with NPC in the U.S., according to a Monday note from Jefferies. IntraBio’s net sales last year, all from Aqneursa in NPC, hit $68 million, according to a company release on Monday.
Just a few weeks ago, IntraBio scored another rare disease approval for Aqneursa, expanding its use to patients with ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T), a prematurely fatal disease that involves the progressive degeneration of the cerebellum. The drug is the first and only treatment to receive approval for A-T worldwide.
IntraBio continues to study Aqneursa in other rare diseases, including GM2 gangliosidoses, inherited cerebellar ataxias and CACNA1A-related disorders. The biotech, founded in 2015 , is also developing treatments for common disorders like migraine and dementias.
Assuming that A-T has a similar patient population to NPC, “sales of several hundred million dollars should be achievable in the US alone,” Jefferies wrote, estimating $1 billion in global peak sales for the drug.
Given this revenue potential, IntraBio’s $2 billion price tag “looks reasonable or slightly undervalued,” the analysts continued, while cautioning that efforts to bolster disease awareness to boost diagnoses “will incur costs.”
For Shionogi, the IntraBio acquisition “offers readily achievable synergies and fits Shionogi’s growth strategy by strengthening its rare disease development capabilities,” Jefferies added.
The Japanese drugmaker’s rare disease portfolio is currently anchored by the ALS drug Radicava. Shionogi acquired Radicava from Tanabe Pharma in December 2025 for $2.5 billion plus certain sales-based royalties. Beyond Radicava, Shionogi also touts rare disease pipeline programs in Fragile X syndrome and Jordan’s syndrome.
Shionogi is actively seeking out M&A opportunities, chairperson and CEO Isao Teshirogi said in August. Aside from IntraBio and Tanabe, the Japanese pharma in May last year moved to absorb Japan Tobacco’s Torii Pharmaceutical for around $1 billion, gaining products such as the atopic dermatitis cream Vtama and the oral drug Miticure for dust mite allergies.
Despite a slowdown in Q3 , 2026 is still shaping up to be a big year for M&A . Recent standout takeovers include Vertex Pharmaceuticals’ acquisition of Crinetics Pharmaceuticals—a deal originally billed to be worth $10 billion but which has been valued at $8.8 billion by S&P Capital IQ, after taking into account debt and other factors. Telix Pharmaceuticals also made waves last month after it revealed designs to absorb the radiopharma specialist ITM Isotope Technologies Munich for $1.65 billion upfront .

At the time, Peter Coratola Jr., founder, president and CEO of EASE Logistics, said deployments like this “help move autonomous trucking from controlled pilots into daily freight operations.”
The Marysville run is EASE’s third autonomous trucking deployment with DriveOhio. It runs under the Truck Automation Corridor Project, an $8.8 million, multi-year initiative the Ohio Department of Transportation, DriveOhio and INDOT launched in 2021 to study truck automation on major routes in both states, according to the companies’ announcement .
EASE put the trucks in service in late August.
The companies said the deployment began generating operational data on safety, reliability and efficiency last month. They plan to use miles driven, loads moved and uptime from daily service to set the next phase and to support scaling talks with ODOT, INDOT and prospective logistics partners. Tuesday’s announcement did not include any of those figures.
“Daily operations in Marysville give us the proof points we need to keep expanding autonomous freight across the corridor and beyond,” said Henrik Green, CTO at Einride.
Closed loop between two warehouses
The trucks shuttle between EASE’s two Marysville facilities.
“Really closed loop right now between our two warehouses, just running things back and forth so we can understand what does it take from a manpower standpoint on either side. You still have to have a human load and unload those things,” Failla said. “But what kind of obstacles does it see navigating around trucks, loading in, loading out, what time frames are best?”
EASE met Einride at a mobility conference in Ohio last year, Failla said. The company’s autonomy work with DriveOhio goes back about four years, and she said the motive was a seat in the regulatory conversation.
“There’s some level of autonomy coming into the freight industry. And what we don’t want is our lawmakers and legislators to decide what that looks like for us without someone who understands the operation at the table,” she said.
Built to the automotive standard
Coratola founded the Dublin, Ohio-based company in 2014 after a first logistics job exposed him to automotive shippers. EASE now hauls food and beverage, CPG, retail and healthcare freight, but its processes were built to what auto plants demand: no-fail freight, overcommunication and the same service at 3 a.m. on a Saturday as at 1 p.m. on a Tuesday, Coratola said in an interview with FreightWaves in August.
An assembly plant can have 1,400 to 2,000 suppliers coming together on a single sequence trailer, he said, and freight that shuts the plant down stops the line.
That supplier base is moving again. OEMs spent two years consolidating around EV production, Coratola said, in some cases going from 2,700 suppliers to about 1,200 and adding plants that can handle lithium. This year he sees production shifting back toward hybrid and internal combustion vehicles, and suppliers that sat dormant for two years are turning back on.
“It looks like their supply chains are reflected more of what people are buying rather than what they think they’re buying,” Coratola said.
Empty racks as the first job
Racks are where Coratola sees autonomy landing first in automotive. Parts arrive at the plant in them, and the empties have to leave. When a supplier runs late or the line falls behind, the empties back up and somebody has to send a driver.
“Rather than holding drivers or continuously having to spot drivers to come get racks, this type of technology would be able to deploy essentially an autonomous supply chain that helps that carousel — racks go back,” Coratola said.
“We’re not talking about sending racks from the Midwest all the way to Texas. We’re talking about getting them out of the plant to a pickup location closer where they can then go on an over-the-road truck,” he said.
The Marysville loop is that carousel at warehouse scale.
Unplanned rack moves are the loads that spike costs, Coratola said, because drivers aren’t always available and the freight gets spotted or expedited. Failla said a carousel could run any time of day, any day of the week, timed around traffic patterns to keep the trucks off congested roads.
Remote operators and the driver question
Remote operators watch the trucks at all times and can take over when one needs a human, Failla said, and EASE is not trying to take jobs from drivers.
“So with the aging population that just is a fact with our drivers, this is also giving them an opportunity to stay in the industry a little bit longer but get them out of that cab,” she said.
Coratola sees drivers and driverless trucks splitting the plant work by whether a load was planned.
“We can reserve the routes that are coming into the plant that are planned for the drivers, and the unplanned routes can be serviced by technologies like this that are running on carousel that might be, in a future state, hopefully less to operate,” Coratola said.

Anduril Industries plans to invest $3.7 billion in a new Maryland shipyard that will manufacture parts for the Navy’s Virginia-class submarines and create 3,100 jobs . The company announced the project Tuesday at Tradepoint Atlantic in Sparrows Point, Baltimore County.
What’s Related
The facility, called Arsenal-2, will cover about 2 million square feet, with initial operations expected in 2030. Permitting will begin immediately, but construction depends on securing the necessary approvals.
The Navy separately awarded Anduril a contract worth up to $2.9 billion, with payments tied to production results. That contract is separate from the company’s planned $3.7 billion private investment.
Anduril plans to start with components such as torpedo tubes before expanding into larger submarine modules and hull sections. General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding will assemble the submarines, with Anduril supplying parts for their production lines.
RELATED: Anduril to Build Giant Drone Factory in Ohio With $310M Grant
Speeding up delays
The project is designed to help address delays in submarine construction by adding another source of critical parts. A senior administration official told reporters that torpedo tubes are among the components holding up Virginia-class submarines already under construction, according to WMAR-2 News .
The Maryland site will occupy 187 acres and include fabrication and assembly areas, production lines, and a 1,200-foot graving dock, a dry dock used for ship work. Production is expected to increase over time after the facility starts operating.
Anduril’s plan comes as the Navy struggles to reach its goal of two Virginia-class submarines annually. Breaking Defense reported that a July Government Accountability Office report identified late supplier deliveries and a shortage of experienced workers as problems slowing the program.
“We need to grow the maritime industrial base, the submarine industrial base, so that we can produce more submarines,” Chris Brose, Anduril’s president and chief strategy officer, told reporters, according to Breaking Defense.
California facility will prepare for Maryland
Anduril also plans to manufacture submarine parts at a new, 160,000-square-foot facility in Orange County, California. That location will give the company a two-year head start on developing manufacturing methods, production workflows, and quality systems before Arsenal-2 begins operating, according to Breaking Defense.
The California operation will make test assets and maritime components, including torpedo tubes, while recruiting and training an early workforce. Anduril says the location will continue other maritime manufacturing work after the Maryland shipyard opens.
For Arsenal-2, the company plans to recruit Baltimore-area workers, including recent high school graduates, vocational program graduates, and people with aerospace or automotive manufacturing experience. Anduril says its training approach is designed to bring in workers without years of shipbuilding experience, WMAR reported.
Incentives need approvals
Maryland and Baltimore County have committed to match up to 13% of Anduril’s anticipated private investment through existing incentives and proposed new funding. New appropriations would require approval from the Maryland General Assembly and Baltimore County Council, according to WMAR.
The county’s proposed contribution includes a personal property tax break worth up to $210 million over 30 years, WYPR reported. Legislation was introduced Monday, with public sessions scheduled for October 13 and 27 before an expected vote in early November.
Arsenal-2 would bring large-scale ship manufacturing back to the former Bethlehem Steel shipyard area. Tradepoint Atlantic purchased the abandoned industrial property in 2014 and has since redeveloped it for logistics businesses , according to WYPR.
